name: Trajectory - projectile motion

summary: Supply the vertical velocity and the ymax and the Trajectory - projectile motion calculator solves for horizontal velocity (vₓ). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Trajectory - projectile motion calculator work?
sections.html:
The Trajectory - projectile motion calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports horizontal velocity (vₓ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the vertical velocity (vᵧ) and the ymax.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in meters per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

sections.title: The formula behind the Trajectory - projectile motion calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Horizontal velocity (vₓ)=velocity × the cosine of (angle of launch (α))
Angle of launch (α)=(vertical velocity (vᵧ) ÷ velocity)
Horizontal velocity (vₓ)=the square root of ((velocity − vertical velocity (vᵧ)) × (velocity + vertical velocity (vᵧ)))
T=(20000 ÷ 196133) × vertical velocity (vᵧ) + (200 ÷ 196133) × the square root of (196133 × initial height (h₀) + 10000 × (vertical velocity (vᵧ) ^ 2))
Horizontal velocity (vₓ)=X ÷ T
Initial height (h₀)=-10000 ÷ 196133 × (vertical velocity (vᵧ) ^ 2) + ymax

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Velocity = 10 m/s and Angle of launch (α) = 10 deg. The calculator returns Horizontal velocity (vₓ) = 9.848078 m/s and Vertical velocity (vᵧ) = 1.736482 m/s.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Horizontal velocity (vₓ) = 9.848078 m/s and Vertical velocity (vᵧ) = 1.736482 m/s should be roughly the size you expected from Velocity = 10 m/s and Angle of launch (α) = 10 deg.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Speed, opening in meters per second

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Trajectory - projectile motion calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the vertical velocity and the ymax — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Trajectory - projectile motion calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns horizontal velocity (vₓ), derived from the vertical velocity and the ymax. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Trajectory - projectile motion calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the vertical velocity and the ymax, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter velocity in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Velocity opens in meters per second and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Horizontal velocity (vₓ) = 9.848078 m/s. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Trajectory - projectile motion calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
